key.notes: hardcoded literal passed to CryptoJS.AES.encrypt as a STRING — so it is a passphrase, not a key: CryptoJS derives a 256-bit key + IV with EVP_BytesToKey(MD5) and an 8-byte random salt, and emits the OpenSSL envelope (wire values start 'U2FsdGVkX1'). Feeding these 16 bytes as a raw key yields garbage.

verified.how: crypto-cli.py dec --structure openssl --kdf evp-md5 --key utf8:<literal> returned the checkout JSON; a re-encrypted body was accepted (200). Cross-checked against the app's own library via scripts/oracle/js-crypto-oracle.js.

notes: One key for every install and every user — the encryption adds no confidentiality against anyone holding the APK. Report it.

A second, legacy path in the same bundle uses a parsed (raw) key with a hardcoded IV: CryptoJS.AES.encrypt(data, enc.Utf8.parse('0123456789abcdef'), {iv: enc.Hex.parse('0011..ff')}) → structure=raw, mode=CBC, key format UTF-8 (AES-128), IV from the literal. Check which endpoints still use it.
The request wrapper is {"request":"<blob>"}; responses are the bare blob, hence whole_body for that direction.
Salt is fresh per message, so identical plaintexts produce different ciphertexts — that is the library, not a design decision by the app.
